summary: This RFC defines an access control model for NETCONF, so access for particular users can be limited to a pre-configured subset of protocol operations and content. It aims at secure, multi-vendor operation. It was replaced by RFC 8341.

plainLanguage.summary: Not every person should be allowed to press every button on a network device. This provides rules saying who can do what. A newer RFC 8341 replaced it.

subtitle: Rules for deciding which NETCONF users may run which operations, touch which data and receive which notifications.

tldr.problem: NETCONF has no standard way to restrict the protocol operations and content that each user is allowed to access.
tldr.mechanism: The NETCONF Access Control Model (NACM) maps users to groups and checks ordered rules at three points: protocol operations, datastore nodes and notifications, with a small CRUDX set of permissions.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6536 was obsoleted by RFC 8341, which is the current definition of NACM.

facts.label: Rule types
facts.value: 4: module, protocol operation, data node, notification

today: RFC 6536 has been obsoleted by RFC 8341, which is now the definition of the NETCONF Access Control Model.

sections.title: The Problem and the Design Goals
sections.content:
The NETCONF protocol does not provide any standard mechanism to restrict the protocol operations and content that each user is authorized to access. This RFC addresses access control for the Operations and Content layers of NETCONF, and gives a YANG data model (ietf-netconf-acm) for configuring it.

Because NETCONF lets new protocol operations be added at any time, the model cannot focus on a fixed set of operations. Instead it protects three conceptual control points: protocol operation (may this operation be invoked), datastore (may these data nodes be read or altered) and notification (may this event type be received).

The goals include simplicity, one set of rules for all three control points, user groups (with group names optionally supplied by a central server such as RADIUS), and the ability to switch enforcement off without deleting rules. Data model designers should also be able to mark sensitive content in a machine-readable way, so it is protected by default.
sections.plainLanguage: A building has three kinds of locked doors: doors to rooms where you do jobs, doors to shelves of files, and a speaker that announces news. This rulebook controls all three doors with the same set of keys.

sections.title: Users, Groups and Rules
sections.content:
A user is identified by a string that is unique within the server, taken from the transport layer when the session is established. If the transport cannot authenticate the user, the session is terminated. Access is granted to a group, and a user can belong to several groups. Group names reported by the transport layer can be used too, if enable-external-groups is true.

There are four kinds of access control rule: a module rule (a whole YANG module), a protocol operation rule, a data node rule (identified by its path) and a notification rule. Rules sit in ordered rule lists that apply to named groups, and each rule says permit or deny.

A server MAY support an emergency recovery session that bypasses all access control, so a broken configuration can be repaired. How it is set up is left to the implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: People are put into teams, and the rulebook talks about teams, not individuals. Each rule says a team is allowed or not allowed to do one thing, and there is a secret emergency key for fixing the rulebook itself.

sections.title: Access Rights and Datastore Behavior
sections.content:
Rights follow a CRUDX model: Create, Read, Update, Delete and eXec (execute a protocol operation). The same rules apply to every datastore, but only the standard candidate, running and startup datastores are controlled. Files reached through the url parameter are not.

For get and get-config, nodes the user cannot read are silently left out of the reply, so filters still work instead of failing with an error. For edit-config, a missing create, delete or update permission on a node makes the operation fail with an access-denied error. If the effective operation on a parent node is none, no access control applies to it, so a user can create a list entry without rights over its parent container.

kill-session is denied by default and needs an explicitly configured rule, because it lets one session disrupt another that is editing a datastore.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask to see a list and some items are secret, you just do not see those items. If you try to change something you are not allowed to change, you get told no.

sections.title: How a Request Is Checked
sections.content:
For each incoming operation the server follows an ordered procedure. It permits the request if enable-nacm is false, if the session is a recovery session, or if the operation is close-session. Otherwise it finds the user's groups, walks the rule lists in order, and uses the first matching rule's permit or deny.

If no rule matches, defaults apply. An operation or node marked nacm:default-deny-all is denied, and a write to a node marked nacm:default-deny-write is denied. Then the global read-default, write-default and exec-default switches decide. The kill-session and delete-config operations are denied unless a rule allows them.

Denied operations produce an access-denied error, and the server MUST NOT put information the client may not read into the error. Denied notifications are simply dropped for that subscription. On first startup with no access control configuration, a server MUST NOT allow write access to any session except a recovery session.
sections.plainLanguage: A guard reads down a checklist from the top and obeys the first line that matches you. If nothing matches, the guard uses the general house rule: let people look, but do not let them change things.

sections.title: The NACM Data Model
sections.content:
The YANG module ietf-netconf-acm holds the global switches, a set of counters and the groups and rule lists. The switches are enable-nacm, read-default, write-default, exec-default and enable-external-groups. Three read-only counters, denied-operations, denied-data-writes and denied-notifications, let a client monitor how often access was refused.

Each group has a name and a list of user names. Each rule-list names the groups it applies to and holds ordered rule entries. Appendix A of the RFC gives configuration examples for module, protocol operation, data node and notification rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook itself is stored as a tidy form with on/off switches, lists of team members and a tally of how many times someone was told no.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists defaults that an administrator should check: enable-nacm defaults to true, read-default to permit, write-default to deny and exec-default to permit. Write access to the access control data should be restricted, and so should read access to it, since it reveals sensitive policy.

Other warnings include rule order (rules are evaluated in the order the client arranged them), editing rules directly in the running datastore without opening unintended access, and trusting external group names. If the protocol that supplies group names does not protect against man-in-the-middle attacks, an attacker might inject group names, and the administrator may set enable-external-groups to false.

A session with some write access can probe for hidden data by repeating edit requests and watching for access-denied errors, which can reveal whether that data exists.
sections.plainLanguage: A rulebook is only safe if the wrong people cannot rewrite it or peek at it. Also, if someone keeps trying doors and hearing who says no, they can guess what is behind them.
